newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - May 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - May 7.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Wednesday:
* In March, orders placed with factories declined 1.6 percent, the biggest drop in seven months.
* Britain's newly-elected Labour government handed control of interests rates to the Bank of England, the country's central bank, cheering the party's opposition.
* Bre-X Minerals shares were dumped after an auditor said its Busang site in Indonesia contained insignificant amounts of gold.

* Chrysler and United Auto Workers negotiators have reached a deal to end a factory engine strike that has shut down the company's production of pickup trucks and Jeep Grand Cherokees for almost a month.
* GTE said it would pay $616 million to acquire Internet service provider BBN Corp and it had formed an alliance with Cisco Systems.
* The Bell Atlantic and NYNEX merger could produce $200 million more in savings than the companies first forecast, but they denied reports they planned to layoff 10,000 workers within five years.
* The Dow industrials rose 10.83 points to close at 7,255.32.

* The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission said Gruntal brokerage firm agreed to pay six former and current female workers $750,000, in a settlement coming from a federal probe into sexual harassment in the workplace.

* Cigarette industry negotiators involved in tobacco settlement talks offered a proposal limiting the kinds of lawsuits smokers could bring but the plan was rejected, according to people familiar with the meeting.

* Newsweek's "Your Child" issue is being recalled because it had a recommendation that parents allow five-month old children feed themselves raw carrot pieces and zweiback crackers by hand, which could cause choking.
* IBM is set to announce that two of its research scientists have devised a computer encryption system that is almost impossible to crack.
* Market place: A takeover fight between H.F. Ahmanson and Washington Mutual for Great Western Financial has a petty element to it.
* California regulators said they would accelerate plans to let utility customers buy electricity from the supplier of their choice by 1998.

* Initial demand for General Motors' new electric car is lackluster at best, as the company figured it would be. But GM is carefully managing initial leasings of the car to make sure the first drivers like the product.
